finding_and_correction: Program description could be misread as effectiveness evidence; retained only as conceptual/implementation evidence.
Effectiveness language in participant perceptions must not be converted into measured clinical effectiveness.
Early applications and author conclusions were bounded as descriptive; no effectiveness claim was retained.
Perceived effectiveness was separated from actual outcome effectiveness and causal inference.
Patient reports were preserved as qualitative findings, not prevalence estimates or causal effects.
Percentages were tied to denominator 19 and not generalized to nurses or public-safety personnel.
PMC article type is article-commentary; the queue's generic Journal Article label must not imply an empirical study.
Perceived better outcomes were not treated as measured consumer outcomes or cost-effectiveness.
Participant endorsement was retained as perception and not upgraded to effectiveness evidence.
Preferences were not converted into evidence that the interventions improve health or implementation outcomes.
